source_evidence.anchor: For p > 0, the p-th moment of X is defined as E X^p, and the p-th absolute moment is E |X|^p.
source_evidence.observation: The source gives two distinct definitions for the same strictly positive order p: an ordinary moment using the signed power X^p and an absolute moment using |X|^p.

source_evidence.anchor: the expectation E X of a random variable X on a probability space (Omega, Sigma, P) is, by definition, the Lebesgue integral of the function X : Omega -> R
source_evidence.observation: The book's measure-theoretic reading treats X as real-valued on a probability space and expectation as Lebesgue integration.

source_evidence.anchor: Throughout this book, we drop the brackets in the notation E[f(X)] and simply write E f(X) instead. Thus, nonlinear functions bind before expectation.
source_evidence.observation: Accordingly, E X^p and E |X|^p mean expectations of the pointwise nonlinear expressions X^p and |X|^p, rather than powers of E X.

source_evidence.anchor: the Lp norm of a random variable: ||X||_Lp = (E |X|^p)^(1/p), p in (0, infinity)
source_evidence.observation: The following display confirms that p ranges over all positive real orders and reuses the absolute moment inside the Lp expression.

binders: A probability space (Omega, Sigma, P) and a real-valued random variable X : Omega -> R (PDF page 1; printed page 5, footnote 1, anchor: "a random variable X on a probability space (Omega, Sigma, P)" and "X : Omega -> R").
A real order p with p > 0 (PDF page 1; printed page 5, Section 1.1, anchor: "For p > 0").
hypotheses: The only condition stated in the defining sentence is strict positivity of p; it states no integrability, finiteness, nonnegativity, or integer-order assumption on X or p (PDF page 1; printed page 5, Section 1.1, anchor: the complete sentence beginning "For p > 0").
conclusions: The p-th moment of X is defined to be E(X^p) (PDF page 1; printed page 5, Section 1.1, anchor: "the p-th moment of X is defined as E X^p").
The p-th absolute moment of X is defined to be E(|X|^p) (PDF page 1; printed page 5, Section 1.1, anchor: "the p-th absolute moment is E |X|^p").
definitions_and_conventions: E denotes expectation, interpreted measure-theoretically as the Lebesgue integral on (Omega, Sigma, P) (PDF page 1; printed page 5, footnote 1, anchor: "expectation E X ... is, by definition, the Lebesgue integral").

Expectation brackets are suppressed and nonlinear functions bind before expectation, so E X^p means E[X^p] and E |X|^p means E[|X|^p] (PDF page 1; printed page 5, footnote 2, anchor: "we drop the brackets" and "nonlinear functions bind before expectation").

The absolute-value bars are present only in the absolute-moment definition, not in the ordinary-moment definition (PDF page 1; printed page 5, Section 1.1, anchor: the paired expressions "E X^p" and "E |X|^p").
implicit_context: Section 1.1 is introducing quantities associated with real random variables (PDF page 1; printed page 5, section heading "Basic quantities associated with random variables" and footnote 1's codomain X : Omega -> R).

The subsequent Lp display uses p in (0, infinity), structurally confirming that the nearby p > 0 convention is not restricted to integers (PDF page 1; printed page 5, anchor: "||X||_Lp = (E |X|^p)^(1/p), p in (0, infinity)").

details: The order p is any strictly positive real number, as stated by p > 0 and reinforced by p in (0, infinity) in the next display (PDF page 1; printed page 5, anchors: "For p > 0" and "p in (0, infinity)").

The ordinary moment applies the power directly to the real-valued X, whereas the absolute moment applies the power to |X| (PDF page 1; printed page 5, Section 1.1, anchor: the contrast between "E X^p" and "E |X|^p").

Both quantities are expectations/Lebesgue integrals of pointwise powers, under the book's bracket-dropping convention (PDF page 1; printed page 5, footnotes 1-2, anchors: "Lebesgue integral" and "nonlinear functions bind before expectation").
The defining sentence supplies no existence or finiteness condition for either expectation (PDF page 1; printed page 5, Section 1.1, anchor: the complete sentence beginning "For p > 0").

undebatable_constraints: p is strictly positive, not explicitly restricted to a natural number or integer (PDF page 1; printed page 5, anchors: "For p > 0" and the subsequent "p in (0, infinity)").
The ordinary p-th moment is written E(X^p), with no absolute value around X (PDF page 1; printed page 5, Section 1.1, anchor: "the p-th moment of X is defined as E X^p").
The p-th absolute moment is written E(|X|^p) (PDF page 1; printed page 5, Section 1.1, anchor: "the p-th absolute moment is E |X|^p").
X is real-valued in the source's measure-theoretic convention, and E is Lebesgue integration (PDF page 1; printed page 5, footnote 1, anchors: "X : Omega -> R" and "Lebesgue integral").
Pointwise exponentiation occurs before expectation; the notation is not (E X)^p (PDF page 1; printed page 5, footnote 2, anchor: "nonlinear functions bind before expectation").
The defining sentence does not state that X is nonnegative or that the relevant expectation is finite (PDF page 1; printed page 5, Section 1.1, anchor: the complete sentence beginning "For p > 0").

ambiguities.issue: For a negative value of the real-valued X and a noninteger real p > 0, the notation X^p has no universally defined real-valued meaning, and this passage gives no convention for it.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 1; printed page 5 combines footnote 1's X : Omega -> R with the unrestricted condition "p > 0" and the expression "E X^p", while separately writing absolute values in "E |X|^p".
ambiguities.impact: The ordinary p-th moment is not fully determined as a real-valued expectation for all random variables and all positive real p; a formalization must either restrict X or p, choose an exponentiation convention, or expose that obstruction.

ambiguities.issue: The passage does not specify existence or finiteness requirements for the expectations used as moments.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 1; printed page 5 defines the moments in the sentence beginning "For p > 0" without an integrability hypothesis; footnote 1 identifies expectation with a Lebesgue integral, and the next paragraph later distinguishes random variables having finite Lp norm.
ambiguities.impact: Depending on the adopted expectation convention, a moment may be extended-valued or may be undefined when integrability fails; the source sentence alone does not choose among these possibilities.

contract_plain_english: For a real-valued random variable X and every real p > 0, the source calls E(X^p) the p-th moment and E(|X|^p) the p-th absolute moment (PDF page 1; printed page 5, Section 1.1, sentence beginning "For p > 0"). Expectation is Lebesgue integration and nonlinear functions bind before E (same page, footnotes 1-2). The statement leaves two semantic points open: how X^p is to be real-valued when X can be negative and p is noninteger, and what existence or finiteness convention is intended for the expectations.
